title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
gist: Two Nature papers on nine hominin teeth from Baxian and Naxian caves in Guangxi, China show Homo erectus survived on mainland Asia until roughly 324,000-184,000 years ago, at least 60,000 years later than previously known, lived in closed-canopy tropical rainforest, travelled up to ~250 km, and likely shared the area with Denisovans. The findings undercut the long-held view that only Homo sapiens could exploit rainforests and that rainforest spread drove H. erectus extinction.

themes.theme: Late survival of Homo erectus in southern China

insights.claim: Luminescence and uranium-series dating of breccia at Baxian and Naxian caves in Guangxi, China places Homo erectus teeth between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, showing the species persisted on mainland Asia at least 60,000 years longer than previously known.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Shows how new dating plus protein methods can rewrite long-standing paleoanthropology timelines.
insights.locator: The hominin teeth and the thousands

insights.claim: Before this find, the youngest mainland-Asian Homo erectus fossils dated to about 420,000-400,000 years ago, while Java populations survived until at least 177,000-108,000 years ago, leaving an unexplained 200,000-300,000-year mainland gap that the Guangxi teeth partly fill.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Context for why the find is significant: it closes a known gap in the fossil record.

insights.claim: Enamel proteins survive far longer than DNA and carry species-identifying variation, enabling researchers to assign four of five sampled teeth from the Guangxi caves to Homo erectus via paleoproteomics.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Ancient protein sequencing is becoming a core tool where DNA is too degraded, extending the reach of molecular anthropology.
insights.quote: Proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA, so they’re more likely to survive a few hundred thousand years.
insights.locator: Proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA

insights.claim: One tooth from Baxian Cave has proteins matching no known Homo erectus variant and a non-erectus shape, which researchers say most likely belonged to a Denisovan, though its proteins do not exactly match any known Denisovan sequence.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Points to co-existence of multiple hominin species in Middle Pleistocene southern China.
insights.quote: strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than Homo erectus in Baxian Cave

insights.claim: Because the cave bones were likely collected by porcupines, whose territories are under about 100 square kilometers, Homo erectus and the probable Denisovan lived in the same general area at around the same time, though any interaction between them is unknown.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Taphonomy (how bones accumulated) constrains how strongly sites can be read as evidence of contact.

insights.claim: Possible Homo sapiens fossils in southern China date to 100,000-120,000 years ago, so for a short window up to three hominin species may have occupied the region's rainforests.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Supports a more crowded, multi-species picture of human evolution in Asia.

insights.claim: An ameloblastin amino-acid substitution unique to the Guangxi Homo erectus teeth marks them as a distinct genetic population, and phylogenetic analysis suggests it may have diverged before the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans split more than 600,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Protein phylogenies can map population structure within extinct hominin species, though data remain sparse.

insights.claim: Carbon isotope ratios in Homo erectus and animal teeth from the Guangxi caves indicate a dense, closed-canopy tropical rainforest resembling today's Amazon, and elevated oxygen-18 points to a warm, wet climate.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Hard isotopic evidence directly challenges assumptions about hominin habitat limits.
insights.locator: Isotopes of the chemical elements carbon

insights.claim: The entrenched view that only Homo sapiens could make a living in tropical rainforests had been used to explain Homo erectus's disappearance as Middle Pleistocene rainforests spread, but the Guangxi evidence shows H. erectus could survive there.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Undercuts a major extinction hypothesis; climate-driven habitat change alone may not explain H. erectus's demise.
insights.quote: even if such habitats did not represent its primary ecological niche

insights.claim: The author argues the findings show scientists have been drastically underestimating Homo erectus's adaptability, though different groups may have varied in how well they coped with spreading rainforests.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a broader reassessment of archaic hominin capabilities.
insights.quote: it does mean that we’ve been drastically underestimating our late cousins

insights.claim: Strontium isotope ratios in enamel show some Guangxi Homo erectus individuals spent childhood (ages ~2-6) as far as 250 km away, matching bedrock in northern Vietnam, mostly through closed-canopy rainforest.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Evidence of long-range movement suggests mobility was routine, not exceptional, for these populations.

insights.claim: Researchers conclude long-distance mobility into rainforest may have been a common behavioural pattern for Homo erectus, and say more stable-isotope work at other Middle Pleistocene sites is needed to test whether this was unique to southern China.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Flags the next research frontier: isotope surveys of other Middle Pleistocene sites.
